summary:
Iraq is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a trans visitor. On 27 April 2024 the Council of Representatives passed an amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution that explicitly criminalises consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression. The President signed the statute on 29 June 2024 and it has been in force since 1 July 2024. The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor and the ILGA Asia briefing of 15 January 2025 both record it as the operative legal baseline.

The penalties are severe. Consensual same-sex relations carry 10 to 15 years' imprisonment. Undergoing or performing a gender-affirming procedure carries 1 to 3 years, which places transition itself outside the law. The statute also penalises the promotion of homosexuality. Reporting by the BBC records supporters framing the law as upholding religious values while rights groups condemned it; Human Rights Watch called for outright repeal on 20 May 2024.

There is no legal framework for gender recognition in Iraq. The 2024 amendment reaches 'biological sex changes based on personal desires and inclination', punishing the transgender person and the doctor alike for up to three years, with court-ordered procedures on intersex people excluded. In practice this closes off change of sex marker on official documentation, so a visitor whose documents do not match their presentation is exposing themselves to a statute with no lawful route around it.

Violence against people perceived as gender-nonconforming is documented and largely unpunished. A CNN report of October 2023 recorded a prominent Iraqi TikToker fatally shot in Baghdad as a crackdown on the LGBTQ community deepened. A BBC investigation found dozens, possibly hundreds, of gay people killed in recent years with authorities turning a blind eye, and recorded the UN assessment that state neglect makes Iraq a perpetrator of the violence rather than merely a bystander. The US State Department's 2012 Human Rights Report for Iraq already documented societal discrimination and violence based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity alongside torture and impunity.

Precedent shows the risk extends to gender expression as such. In early 2012 a wave of killings targeted 'emo' teenagers accused of homosexuality on the strength of their clothing and hairstyle; the attacks were carried out by Shi'a death squads of the Mahdi Army, and flyers distributed in Baghdad named individuals and threatened them unless they cut their hair and abandoned non-conformist dress.

Removal is a stated consequence of criminalised status: the 2024 law is applied with fines and deportation, so a trans visitor who comes to official attention risks expulsion as well as prosecution.
tangentialFactors:
Foreign governments treat Iraq as a country where LGBT+ people face a real risk of persecution. The UK Home Office's Country Policy and Information Note on Iraq covering sexual orientation and gender identity and expression, version 3.0 of July 2025, assesses risk from state and hybrid actors and from non-state actors, and addresses protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims. That assessment sits alongside a longer record: the US State Department's 2012 Human Rights Report documented sectarian violence, torture and impunity together with discrimination and violence against individuals on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity grounds.

The violence documented against gay Iraqis is not confined to any single period or faction. The 2012 'emo killings' and the targeted shooting of a visible online figure in Baghdad in October 2023 belong to the same pattern of public targeting with subsequent impunity, a pattern the BBC investigation described as a documented culture of abuse in which authorities decline to investigate. Organised militia involvement in the earlier round of killings indicates that the threat can come from armed actors operating outside state control as well as from the state itself.

Adjacent statutory provisions compound the exposure. The Iraqi Personal Status Law of 1959, amended in 1981, permits a wife to divorce her husband where he is guilty of a homosexual relationship, treating it as infidelity, and both that law and the Kurdistan Personal Status Law of 1992 define marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are therefore unavailable. The 1986 decision by the former ruler to relocate all Iraqis living with AIDS to a special prison facility is part of the same history of state response to sexual health and sexuality through detention.
localsOnly:
Iraqi residents have no legal route to change the sex marker on official documents. The 2024 amendment prohibits gender-change procedures undertaken on personal desire or inclination for up to three years against both the individual and the physician, and the only stated exception covers court-ordered procedures on intersex people. Legal sex-change documentation is effectively unavailable.

Marriage is governed by the Iraqi Personal Status Law 1959, whose Article 3 defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman; the Kurdistan Personal Status Law 1992 does the same in Article 7 of its own definition of marriage. Article 7 of the 1959 law additionally requires couples seeking to marry to produce medical documents showing they are not infected with AIDS. The 1981 amendment to the Personal Status Law allows a wife to divorce a husband found guilty of a homosexual relationship, treated as infidelity.

Support for Iraqi LGBTQ people is delivered overwhelmingly by NGOs rather than by the state. Iraqi LGBT, established in September 2005, works on relocating LGBTQ people to safer countries, provides legal help for asylum seekers and maintains safe houses inside Iraq. The International Railroad for Queer Refugees, founded in 2008, supplies financial and resettlement assistance to LGBTQ asylum seekers fleeing persecution on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Iraqueer, formed in March 2015, runs education work including published security and health-safety guides, videos and workshops on gender and sexuality, and advocacy during crises.

Advocacy organisations have also shifted shelter access. OWFI led more than 40 local organisations in changing Iraq's Anti-Shelter Policy, which had permitted only government-run shelters to operate. Rasan expanded its projects from 2016 as a partner of COC Nederland in the Pride Program, known locally as Crossing Iraqi Rainbow.
outOfScopeNotes:
The parliamentary vote is dated 27 April 2024 by Human Rights Watch and the Library of Congress, while the ILGA Asia briefing gives 28 April 2024. The discrepancy is unresolved in the sources reviewed; the presidential signature on 29 June 2024 and entry into force on 1 July 2024 are consistent across them.

Whether the fines and deportation reported alongside the 15-year maximum apply to visitors as opposed to residents is not separately sourced. The characterisation of removal as a stated consequence of criminalised status rests on a single overview source and is not corroborated by an immigration instrument in the inventory.

Enforcement in the Kurdistan Region under the 1992 Personal Status Law and its relationship to the 2024 federal amendment is not addressed by any source here, and no reporting in the inventory records a prosecution of a foreign national under the new statute. The figures of 'dozens, possibly hundreds' of killings come from one BBC investigation and have not been independently reconciled with any official Iraqi count; no state casualty record appears in the inventory.
